prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated at once, bringing optical frequency standards to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B033 to B053, and I want to be exact about why. My round-1 case for twisted bilayer graphene rested on originality, and I still hold that the flat-band prediction and the correlated phases are real and reproduced. What moved me is the combination of three things the exchange has made plain. First, the credit for B033 cannot be repaired inside the supplied names: Yuan Cao, who carried the decisive 2018 experiments, and other moire pioneers cannot be added, and four colleagues (Lindroth, Mehlig, Pearce, Kroll) independently put the same maturity concern, namely an unsettled pairing mechanism and device variability. I think the core is stable, but a prize should not rest on a case where the committee has to argue away both the credit gap and the open mechanism at once. Second, the chair's synthesis shows that B053 is the only candidate every member either prefers or names as a fallback, and that its support comes from atomic, condensed-matter, particle and astroparticle backgrounds; I do not treat the count as a substitute for judgment, but it tells me the scientific case survives scrutiny from outside the specialty of its supporters. Third, on the substance: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light shift that would otherwise forbid tight confinement of many atoms, and Ye's group turned that into many-atom interrogation near 1e-18, independently matched at several national laboratories. A two-name credit maps onto it. The citation should be written around the lattice scheme and its precision realisation, so that it says what is new relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize.
statement.case_against: The reservations I carried in round 1 have not gone away and I do not want to hide them. A clock is a measurement instrument, and I still regard the main payoff, a redefined second and sensitive tests of constants and the dark sector, as prospective rather than delivered; Johansson is right that the case should not rest on redefinition, and I agree. The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlled single ions is real, and I think Mehlig is right to press it. I have not been persuaded that the overlap is disqualifying, because trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength is a separate step from either, but I would want the citation to say so plainly. The two names also leave out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and other clock groups, and the relative weight of Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy programme cannot be settled from the supplied material. Finally, I am giving up the candidate in my own field that I think has the greater conceptual novelty, so my move reflects a judgment on maturity and credit, not a claim that precision measurement is more important than a new regime of correlated matter.

responses.point: Prefers B053 on clean attribution, 1e-18 uncertainties and global reproduction, writes the citation around magic-wavelength trapping, and would let twisted bilayer graphene settle before honouring it.
responses.response: In round 1 I resisted your maturity argument; having read the whole exchange I now accept most of it. My view of the physics of B033 is unchanged, since the flat bands and correlated insulators are reproduced across many groups, but your point that the mechanism and the missing experimental first author cannot both be handled in one citation is correct. I also agree with the shape of your citation: it should rest on magic-wavelength lattice trapping of neutral atoms and the accuracy it enabled. Where I would add a caution is the credit between the two names. Your reading, Katori for the proposal and first strontium lattice clock and Ye for accuracy and the many-body regime, is a fair description of contributions, but the citation should not rank them, and should not read as a prize for the whole field of optical clocks.

responses.point: Moved B053 to first place but keeps B009 as first alternative, arguing that if discovery in the strict sense outweighs invention, IceCube is the stronger candidate, and warns that B033 carries an attribution gap the committee cannot repair.
responses.response: I agree with you on B033: the missing Cao credit is exactly the kind of gap the supplied names cannot close, and that was a main reason I moved. On the discovery-versus-invention question, I do not think the statute forces a ranking. An invention that changes what can be measured by two orders of magnitude is within the statutory language, and it has been honoured before. I would not set B009 against it on that ground alone. Where I would join you is that the choice should be made on whether B009 can be allocated among Halzen, Karle and Spiering without a defensible fourth voice, and the diffuse flux against source identification, which you and Danielsson read differently. I cannot resolve that from the supplied material, and I leave B009 outside my alternatives for that reason.

responses.point: Prefers B013 as a durable organising principle and says the 2016 prize did not cover the quantum spin Hall prediction, Z2 classification or HgTe observation; in round 1 he also remarked that the lattice-clock overlap is closer than the 2016 overlap with B013.
responses.response: Your distinction on the 2016 prize is useful and I take it more seriously than I did in round 1: the Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz citation concerned topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall plateaus, and the Z2 spin Hall prediction and the HgTe edge transport are a separate prediction-then-observation sequence. That makes the overlap smaller than I stated. The obstacle I still cannot get past is credit, not merit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe structure Molenkamp measured, and Hasan's three-dimensional work is outside any three-name set. I keep B013 as my second alternative. On your point that the lattice-clock overlap is closer, I disagree in degree: the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured a tool and a class of single-ion control, while the lattice scheme, with many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, is the step neither provides.

responses.point: Prefers B053, names Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's many-atom interrogation near 1e-18, and flags his time in Hall's laboratory and the 2005 and 2012 overlaps.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked whether you would rank B053 above B033 if moire matter were judged a new regime rather than a technique. I now think I framed it wrongly: I would give B033 that standing, but that does not settle ordering when the credit is incomplete and the mechanism is open. I agree with your reading that independent comparison among JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE at the 1e-18 level is what makes the result stable, and I would not put the main weight on a future redefinition of the second. Your disclosure about Hall's laboratory seems to me proportionate; it concerns an enabling tool rather than the credited names.

responses.point: Prefers the experimental Higgs discovery for Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee, accepts that allocation among thousands is the difficulty, and would not resist B053 if that allocation cannot be made defensible.
responses.response: I regard the scientific case for B046 as overwhelming and I did not rank it first only because of the allocation: three of Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra cannot represent two collaborations without a leadership-based choice that I do not believe the committee can defend on the supplied material, and the roles at the time of the announcement are unverified. Your own statement that you would accept B053 if the allocation fails seems to me the right test, and on my reading it fails, so we reach the same fallback. If you or others can state a defensible selection principle, for example by naming the founders of the two proposals rather than the spokespersons, I would reconsider; I have not seen one yet.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a metrology achievement as a discovery or invention of equal standing to a new regime of matter, which is a judgment, not a fact I can establish.
Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes make B053 too close to earlier recognition; I think the lattice scheme is separable but I cannot prove it.
How to word the citation so it neither subordinates Ye's accuracy programme to Katori's proposal nor the reverse, and does not overreach into ion-clock territory.
Whether B033 will look clearer in a few years once the pairing mechanism and device variability settle, which would change my ordering later.
I rely on memory for dates, priority, clock uncertainty figures and roles and have not verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile, and B053 lies outside my research area of electronic structure and magnetism. B033 and B013 are close to my own field and B052 supplies data used by materials theory; I have moved away from my field's candidate, so that proximity no longer favours my preferred configuration, though I keep it on record. I also served as chair for the 2025 cycle, which may colour my view of B001, which I do not support. I report no personal tie to any credited person.
